scope: One additional fish for the species guide, illustrative reef encounters and optional identification activity. The model represents one yellow-to-ochre adult appearance documented in Singapore, not a fixed colour phase or a composite of several seahorse species. New copy is paraphrased from museum, government, specialist and primary-research accounts.
iucnYearConvention: Use the actual assessment year, 2012, reported as 16 August 2012 by FishBase's current IUCN 2025-2 export. The IUCN specialist group's current table independently lists Vulnerable and a latest publication year of 2014. Its adjacent 2019 entry means next scheduled reassessment, not a later assessment. The direct IUCN page/PDF was inaccessible, so no successful direct full-assessment access is claimed. Retain the publication year separately.

specimens.name: Spotted seahorse
marks: Deep, upright body with a horse-like head and thick tubular snout
A low, rounded crown bends toward the back of the head
Armoured body rings bear low rounded bumps rather than long sharp spines
A long gripping tail can coil around a holdfast and has no tail fin
specimens.role: Small predator of planktonic crustaceans in coastal food webs.
specimens.fact: The male carries developing young in a brood pouch and releases them as tiny seahorses.
specimens.habitat: Indo-West Pacific coastal habitats, including Singapore estuaries with seagrass and macroalgae over silty sand. It also occurs around sheltered sandy and reef habitats.
specimens.diet: Tiny crustaceans and other zooplankton, drawn through the tubular snout by suction.
specimens.behavior: Often grips vegetation or another support with its prehensile tail. Small dorsal and pectoral fins help it move and steer; it can leave its holdfast to swim.
specimens.observe: Compare the upright trunk and curled gripping tail with the banded pipefish’s slender body and distinct tail fin. Then inspect the rounded crown and thick snout. Yellow is only one appearance: Singapore adults also occur in greenish brown with dark dots.

claimSupport.acceptedName: The current indexed California Academy of Sciences catalog accepts Hippocampus kuda Bleeker, 1852. Its Singapore type locality and the NUS Singapore observation anchor the chosen representation. The same current catalog accepts H. taeniopterus separately; older broad synonymies and Australian common-seahorse accounts are not merged into this model.
claimSupport.marks: The NUS field record supports the rear-turned coronet, thick snout and absence of sharp nose/body spines. The Project Seahorse identification guide supports the low rounded crown, bony rings and prehensile tail without a caudal fin. These are combined teaching marks, not a sufficient field diagnosis among all seahorses.
claimSupport.roleDiet: The CMFRI account supports zooplankton suction feeding. The Waikīkī aquarium's primary husbandry observations independently identify crustacean plankton as food; captive prey examples are not treated as a complete wild diet.
claimSupport.factBehavior: CMFRI describes the adult male brood pouch. The Waikīkī general seahorse account supports tail attachment, dorsal/pectoral propulsion and miniature young. The illustrated holdfast posture is not a claim of permanent immobility or lifelong exclusive pairing.
claimSupport.colourStage: NUS identified adult photographs support yellow through green-brown Singapore appearances, including dark dots. The representative is an unsexed, non-pregnant adult. Neither yellow colour nor dark spots imply a particular sex or life stage, and no juvenile-to-adult colour rule is invented.
claimSupport.sizeDepth: The 12 cm nominal display height is an illustrative adult scale. Project Seahorse gives a recorded adult height of 17 cm and CMFRI gives 7–17 cm using a tail-tip-to-coronet convention. FAO separately reports 30 cm stretched total length. Camins et al. Table 5 gives an IUCN interval of 0–55 m and newer iSeahorse observations of 0–45 m; FishBase's broader 0–68 m entry is retained as an explicit disagreement, not silently capped.
claimSupport.iucn: The current IUCN specialist-group table lists VU, latest published assessment 2014, next reassessment due 2019. FishBase's current IUCN export reports an assessment date of 16 August 2012. A missed reassessment target is not evidence of a new assessment.
claimSupport.comparison: The one-way banded_pipefish link contrasts body orientation, tail function and presence of a caudal fin. Its existing record and references remain unchanged. Both fishes are syngnathids; the teaching comparison does not imply that a pipefish is the nearest seahorse lookalike.

specimens.caution: Hippocampus kuda has a complicated species-complex history. Older accounts apply the name more broadly than some current museum taxonomies, so the public habitat avoids a disputed country-by-country global list. Colour varies and is not a reliable species key. Do not import Australian H. taeniopterus photographs, long spines of other seahorses, a dorsal mane, ordinary fish scales or a tail fin. The generic seahorse silhouette alone cannot establish H. kuda in the wild. Regional Singapore Red List categories are not the global IUCN category. Posed height and straightened length are different measurements. The 0–55 m source interval is not an experimentally established physiological limit.

modelProvenance.nominalDimension: Approximate displayed upright height, with the tail curled naturally; not straightened total length
modelProvenance.representative: An unsexed, non-pregnant yellow-to-ochre Singapore adult with restrained dark mottling. This is one documented variable appearance rather than a fixed regional phase, sex marker or colour-based species diagnosis.
modelProvenance.basis: Nominal 12 cm is an illustrative posed model dimension chosen within the published adult size scale. It is not equated with extended tail-to-coronet height, NUS vent-to-coronet body height, or FAO stretched total length. Registry depth 0–55 m follows the IUCN interval tabulated in primary 2024 research; a broader FishBase 0–68 m record and older FAO approximately 30 m account remain disclosed. Typical sheltered shallow-water placement does not assert that every depth or reef substrate is equally suitable.
modelProvenance.anatomy: Deep upright ring-armoured trunk; bent neck; thick tubular snout ending in a tiny mouth; mobile eyes; low rounded rear-overhanging coronet; low blunt ring tubercles; small dorsal fin on the back and paired pectoral fins behind the head; long prehensile tail without a caudal fin. A small subordinate illustrative holdfast stem makes the tail's actual fixed contact legible.
modelProvenance.anatomyLimits: No long body thorns, leaflike appendages, mane, ordinary fish scales or tail fin. Fine ray/ring counts may be simplified and are not a field-identification key. No male pouch or pregnancy state is assigned. Warm colour is pigmentation, not fluorescence or a special spectral-vision claim.
modelProvenance.motion: Conservative bottom/base placement beside rubble with a rooted holdfast and fixed gripping tail. Gentle dorsal/pectoral fin movement and subtle upper-body motion may suggest water movement while keeping the grip stationary. This illustrative encounter does not imply the species never releases its tail, swims or changes location.
